## Jump‑in: Your First Design Sprint in Figma  

Imagine you’ve just been hired to mock‑up a landing page for a new coffee‑subscription startup. The deadline is tomorrow, the client wants to see a clickable prototype, and you’ve never opened Figma before. Where do you start?  

In the next few minutes you’ll open a fresh Figma file, locate the panels that will become your command centre, learn the vocabulary that designers use every day, and flip between pages to organise your work. By the end of this chapter you’ll be comfortable enough to open a new project, move around the interface, and talk about **frames**, **layers**, and **components** with confidence.

---

## 1. The Figma Workspace at a Glance  

When you first log in to Figma (either via the web at figma.com or the desktop app) you land on the **Dashboard** – a gallery of recent files and teams. Clicking **New File** opens the **Editor**, the canvas where all design activity happens. The editor is divided into several distinct zones; each one serves a specific purpose.

### 1.1 Toolbar (Top)

The thin horizontal bar that stretches across the top of the window contains the most frequently used tools:

| Icon | Name | Quick use |
|------|------|-----------|
| ![Move tool](https://via.placeholder.com/12) | **Move** | Click‑drag to reposition objects; also the default cursor. |
| ![Frame tool](https://via.placeholder.com/12) | **Frame** | Create containers that can hold other objects – the backbone of any layout. |
| ![Rectangle, Ellipse, etc.](https://via.placeholder.com/12) | **Shape tools** | Draw rectangles, circles, polygons, lines, and arrows. |
| ![Pen tool](https://via.placeholder.com/12) | **Pen** | Sketch custom vector paths. |
| ![Text tool](https://via.placeholder.com/12) | **Text** | Add typographic content. |
| ![Slice tool](https://via.placeholder.com/12) | **Slice** | Mark export‑ready sections (used later). |
| ![Comment icon](https://via.placeholder.com/12) | **Comment** | Drop sticky‑note comments for collaboration. |
| **Zoom controls** | – | Zoom in/out or fit canvas to window. |
| **Undo / Redo** | – | Standard shortcuts (⌘Z / ⌘ShiftZ). |

Most of these icons expand into sub‑menus when you click and hold, revealing extra options (e.g., the Shape tools let you choose between rectangle, line, arrow, etc.).

### 1.2 Layers Panel (Left)

The vertical column on the left lists every **layer** in your file, arranged hierarchically. Think of it as the “outline” of your design:

- **Pages** sit at the top level. Each page holds its own collection of frames and objects.
- **Frames** appear as bold entries; they can contain other layers.
- **Objects** (shapes, text, images) are indented under the frame that houses them.

You can drag items to reorder them, nest objects inside frames, or hide/show layers using the eye icon. The panel also includes a **search bar** to quickly locate a layer by name.

### 1.3 Properties Panel (Right)

When you select any object, the **Properties Panel** on the right updates to show context‑specific controls:

- **Design tab** – fill colour, stroke, effects, opacity, layout grids, constraints.
- **Prototype tab** – interaction triggers, destinations, animation types.
- **Inspect tab** – CSS, iOS, Android code snippets for developers (useful later).

At the very top of this panel sits the **File name** (editable) and a **Share** button for collaboration.

### 1.4 Bottom Bar (Status)

The thin bar at the bottom displays helpful information such as the current **zoom level**, cursor coordinates, and a **progress indicator** when assets are loading.

### 1.5 Keyboard Shortcuts – Your Speed Boost

Figma is built for keyboard efficiency. A few that you’ll use immediately:

| Shortcut | Action |
|----------|--------|
| **A** | Select **Frame** tool |
| **R** | Select **Rectangle** tool |
| **T** | Select **Text** tool |
| **V** | Activate **Move** (hand) tool |
| **Shift + A** | Insert **Component** from assets |
| **⌘ + /** (or **Ctrl + /**) | Open **Quick actions** (search any command) |
| **⌘ + G** | **Group** selected layers |
| **⌘ + Shift + G** | **Ungroup** |
| **⌘ + /** | **Duplicate** selected layer |
| **⌘ + 1** | **Zoom to fit** the canvas |
| **⌘ + 2** | **Zoom to selection** |

Feel free to keep a cheat‑sheet nearby until the shortcuts become second nature.

---

## 2. Core Terminology – What’s What?  

Before you start dragging objects onto the canvas, it helps to internalise the language designers use. The three terms below appear in virtually every design conversation.

### 2.1 Frames  

A **frame** is a container that can hold other layers—shapes, text, images, even other frames. It is the digital equivalent of a piece of paper or a screen. Frames are essential because:

- They define **boundaries** for layout (e.g., a desktop screen is a 1440 × 1024‑pixel frame).
- They enable **constraints** (how child objects behave when the frame is resized).
- They can be turned into **components** (reusable UI modules) later on.

When you click the Frame tool (A) and drag on the canvas, you are creating a new frame. You can also convert an existing group of layers into a frame via **Right‑click → Frame selection**.

### 2.2 Layers  

Every visual element in Figma lives on a **layer**. Layers are stacked from bottom to top; the higher a layer sits in the list, the more it appears in front of lower layers. Layers can be:

- **Primitive** – simple shapes, text blocks, images.
- **Group** – a collection of layers that move together, but are not a frame.
- **Component instance** – a copy of a reusable component (covered later).

Understanding the layer hierarchy is crucial for managing overlap, applying effects, and troubleshooting why something isn’t appearing where you expect.

### 2.3 Components  

A **component** is a master design element that you can reuse across your file. Think of it as a “template” that lives in the **Assets** panel. When you drag a component onto the canvas you create an **instance**. Changing the master component updates all its instances automatically—a powerful way to keep UI consistent.

For now, you only need to recognise components when you see them in the **Assets** panel or when a layer has a **diamond‑shaped icon** next to its name. Creating your own components will be covered in Chapter 5.

---

## 3. Creating Your First File  

Now that the workspace and vocabulary are clear, let’s walk through the practical steps of opening a fresh file, naming it, and setting up a basic structure for our coffee‑subscription landing page.

### 3.1 Starting a New File  

1. **From the Dashboard**: Click the **+ New File** button in the top‑right corner.  
2. **From the Desktop App**: Choose **File → New** from the menu bar.  

A blank canvas appears with a single default page named **Page 1**.

> **Tip:** If you prefer to work offline, the desktop app stores files locally and syncs when you reconnect to the internet.

### 3.2 Naming the File  

At the top of the editor you’ll see “Untitled.” Click on the text and type a descriptive name, for example:

```
CoffeeCo – Landing Page – v1
```

Renaming early helps you locate the file later, especially as your library of projects grows.

### 3.3 Adding and Organising Pages  

Pages let you separate distinct flows or design stages (e.g., “Wireframes,” “High‑Fidelity,” “Prototype”). To add a new page:

1. In the **Layers Panel**, locate the **Pages** section at the very top.  
2. Click the **+** icon next to “Page 1.”  
3. A new page appears (automatically named **Page 2**). Double‑click the name to rename it, e.g., **Home‑Screen**.

You can reorder pages by dragging them up or down, or delete a page (right‑click → **Delete**) if it’s no longer needed.

### 3.4 Navigating Between Pages  

Switching pages is as simple as clicking their names in the Layers panel. For keyboard lovers:

- **⌘ + Option + 1** (or **Ctrl + Alt + 1**) jumps to the first page.  
- **⌘ + Option + 2**, **⌘ + Option + 3**, etc., move you to subsequent pages.

When you’re on a page, the canvas only shows the frames and layers belonging to that page, keeping your workspace uncluttered.

### 3.5 Setting Up a Frame for the Landing Page  

1. Select the **Frame** tool (**A**).  
2. In the **Properties Panel**, under **Design → Size**, choose a preset size such as **Desktop – 1440 × 1024**.  
3. Click anywhere on the canvas to place the frame. It will appear as a rectangular outline with a faint blue background.  

Rename the frame to **Home‑Desktop** (double‑click its name in the Layers panel). This naming convention—*screen‑device*—helps you locate frames quickly later on.

### 3.6 Adding Basic Layers  

Let’s sketch a quick header:

1. **Rectangle** (**R**) → drag across the top of the frame, height ≈ 80 px.  
2. **Fill** → pick a coffee‑brown colour (#5A381E).  
3. **Text** (**T**) → click inside the rectangle, type “CoffeeCo.” Change the font to **Montserrat Bold**, size = 24 pt, colour = white.  

Now you have a simple header layer inside your frame. In the Layers panel it will appear as:

```
Home‑Desktop
 └─ Header (Rectangle)
    └─ CoffeeCo (Text)
```

Notice how the text layer is **nested** under the rectangle because you created it while the rectangle was selected. Nesting keeps related items together and makes it easier to move the whole header as a unit later.

---

## 4. Exploring the Interface While Designing  

With a frame and a couple of layers in place, you can start to feel the rhythm of Figma. Below are a few common actions you’ll perform while building a prototype, each illustrated with the coffee‑subscription example.

### 4.1 Selecting and Moving Objects  

- **Click** on any layer in the canvas or the Layers panel to select it.  
- **Drag** the selection to reposition it. Holding **Shift** while dragging constrains movement to 45‑degree angles.  
- Press **⌘ + D** (or **Ctrl + D**) to **duplicate** the selected layer—useful for creating a navigation menu from the header.

### 4.2 Resizing Frames and Objects  

- Hover over the edges of a frame or shape until the cursor turns into a double‑arrow.  
- Drag to resize; hold **Shift** to keep proportions.  
- For frames, the **Properties Panel** also shows numeric width/height fields—type exact values for precision.

### 4.3 Adjusting Layer Order  

If your text disappears behind the rectangle, you’ve hit a **stacking** issue. Resolve it by:

- Selecting the text layer, then choosing **⌘ + ]** (bring forward) or **⌘ + [** (send backward).  
- Or, simply drag the layer up or down in the Layers panel.

### 4.4 Using the Quick Actions Menu  

Press **⌘ + /** (or **Ctrl + /**) to open the **Quick Actions** search bar. Start typing “stroke” and you’ll instantly see options to add or edit strokes, even if you’re not currently on a shape. This feature speeds up workflow dramatically once you get used to it.

### 4.5 Previewing Your Design  

At any moment, click the **Present** button (play icon) in the top‑right corner to open a full‑screen preview of the current page. This is especially helpful for checking alignment and visual hierarchy without the distraction of UI chrome.

---

## 5. Practical Walk‑through: Building a Simple Landing Page Skeleton  

Let’s expand the header into a minimal but functional landing page. Follow each step; feel free to experiment with colours or spacing to make the design your own.

### 5.1 Hero Section  

1. **Add a new rectangle** (R) below the header, spanning the full width of the frame, height ≈ 500 px.  
2. Set **Fill** to a light coffee‑cream colour (#F3E5D8).  
3. **Insert Text** (T) centred vertically inside the rectangle: “Your Coffee, Delivered Fresh.”  
   - Font: **Montserrat Semi‑Bold**, size = 36 pt, colour = #3A2E2A.  
4. Below that, add a **Button**:  
   - Rectangle ≈ 200 × 50 px, Fill = #5A381E, Corner radius = 8 px.  
   - Text inside: “Start Free Trial”, Font = Montserrat Medium, size = 16 pt, colour = white.  

Group the button elements (⌘ + G) and name the group **CTA‑Button**. This keeps the rectangle and text together for easy repositioning.

### 5.2 Feature Cards  

1. **Duplicate** the CTA‑Button group (⌘ + D) and place the copy below the hero section, leaving a margin of 80 px.  
2. Change its label to “Learn More”. Adjust the fill colour to a softer brown (#7A5230).  
3. Create three **Feature Card** frames (A → Frame) each 300 × 200 px, spaced evenly across the width.  
   - Inside each frame, add an **Icon** (use the built‑in **Assets → Icons** later) and a short description.  
   - Name the frames **Feature‑1**, **Feature‑2**, **Feature‑3**.  

You now have a basic skeleton: header, hero, call‑to‑action, and three feature cards. All elements sit inside the **Home‑Desktop** frame, keeping the design tidy.

### 5.3 Organising Layers for Clarity  

- Select the **Home‑Desktop** frame, then click the **Layers** panel’s **⋮** menu and choose **Collapse all**. This collapses sub‑layers, giving you a high‑level view.  
- To further organise, create a **Group** called **Header‑Group** containing the header rectangle and logo text.  
- Likewise, group the hero background, headline, and CTA‑Button into **Hero‑Group**.  

Consistent naming and grouping make it far easier to locate elements later—especially when you return to the file after a break.

---

## 6. Going Beyond the Basics: Next Steps  

You now have a functional Figma file with:

- A clear understanding of the **toolbar**, **layers panel**, and **properties panel**.  
- Mastery of the core terms **frames**, **layers**, and **components** (recognising components even if you haven’t created one yet).  
- The ability to **create a new file**, **rename it**, **add pages**, **navigate** between them, and **build a simple layout**.

From here you can explore:

- **Frames vs. Groups** – when to use each.  
- **Assets panel** – importing icons, images, and eventually your own components.  
- **Design tab controls** – colours, gradients, effects, layout grids (which will be the focus of Chapter 3).  

The next chapter will dive into **setting up frames and pages** more strategically, introducing layout grids and guides that help you align content precisely.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The **toolbar**, **layers panel**, and **properties panel** form the core of the Figma workspace; each serves a distinct purpose.  
- **Frames** are containers that define screen boundaries; **layers** are every visual element; **components** are reusable master objects.  
- Creating a new file involves clicking **New File**, naming the file, adding pages, and setting up a primary frame for your design.  
- Navigation between pages is done via the **Pages** list or keyboard shortcuts (**⌘ + Option + <number>**).  
- Organising layers with clear names, groups, and hierarchy keeps your design tidy and speeds up later work.  

With these fundamentals, you’re ready to move from a blank canvas to a structured design ready for deeper layout work and prototyping. Happy designing!

## Why Pages and Frames Matter for Web Prototypes  

Imagine you’ve just landed a freelance contract to design a multi‑page corporate website. The client wants to see concepts for the **home page**, a **product showcase**, a **blog**, and a **contact form**—each with a desktop, tablet, and mobile version. Without a clear structure, you’ll quickly lose track of which screen belongs to which device, and you’ll spend precious minutes hunting through a tangled canvas.  

Pages and frames are Figma’s built‑in filing system. **Pages** let you separate whole design phases (e.g., *Wireframes → High‑Fidelity Mockups → Final Assets*). **Frames** act like digital canvases that mimic real device screens, keeping your layers organized and your design scalable. Mastering these two tools early saves you from chaos later and lets you focus on creativity instead of file management.

---

## 1. Adding and Renaming Pages  

### 1.1 The purpose of pages in a web‑design workflow  
- **Design phases** – Keep early sketches separate from polished mockups.  
- **Team collaboration** – Others can jump to the relevant section without scrolling through unrelated artboards.  
- **Version control** – Quickly compare iterations by toggling page visibility.

### 1.2 Creating a new page  

1. Open the **Dashboard** and double‑click a project to open the **Editor** (you already know how to start a new file).  
2. In the left‑hand **Layers** panel, locate the **Pages** list at the top.  
3. Click the **+** button next to “Pages.” A new page appears named *Page 1* by default.

> **Tip:** If you’re working on a brand‑new website, start with three pages: **Wireframes**, **Mockups**, and **Assets**. You can always add more later.

### 1.3 Renaming a page  

1. Double‑click the page name (e.g., *Page 1*).  
2. Type a descriptive label, such as *Wireframes – Desktop* or *Mockups – Mobile*.  
3. Press **Enter** to confirm.

> **Pro tip:** Use a consistent naming convention like `Phase – Device`. This pattern makes the file searchable via the **search bar** and instantly tells collaborators what they’re looking at.

### 1.4 Reordering and duplicating pages  

- **Reorder:** Drag a page up or down in the list to change its position. The order you set is the order shown in the **Layers** panel, which can help you prioritize work.  
- **Duplicate:** Right‑click a page and select **Duplicate**. This creates a copy with all its frames and layers intact—perfect for branching a design direction without altering the original.

---

## 2. Building Frames for Common Device Sizes  

### 2.1 What a frame really is  

In the previous chapter you learned that a **frame** is a container that can hold other objects, similar to a group but with its own dimensions and properties. For web design, frames become your *artboards*—each one represents a specific screen size.

### 2.2 Selecting a preset device size  

1. Choose the **Frame** tool (shortcut **F**) from the toolbar.  
2. In the **Properties Panel** under the **Design** tab, you’ll see a dropdown labeled **Preset**.  
3. Click the dropdown and scroll to the **Desktop**, **Tablet**, and **Mobile** sections. Common options include:  
   - **Desktop – 1440 × 1024** (large desktop)  
   - **Tablet – 768 × 1024** (portrait)  
   - **Mobile – 375 × 812** (iPhone X/11 Pro)  

Selecting a preset instantly resizes the frame to the exact dimensions you need.

### 2.3 Custom device frames  

If your project targets a non‑standard screen (e.g., a 1366 × 768 laptop), you can:  

1. Click the **Frame** tool and draw a rectangle on the canvas.  
2. With the frame selected, go to the **Properties Panel** and manually enter the width and height values.  

> **Note:** You can also name the frame directly in the **Layers** panel, e.g., *Desktop – 1366*.

### 2.4 Organizing frames within a page  

A good practice is to keep all frames for the same device on a single page:

| Page name | Contains |
|-----------|----------|
| **Wireframes – Desktop** | All desktop‑size frames (home, product, blog, contact) |
| **Wireframes – Tablet** | Tablet‑size frames for each page |
| **Wireframes – Mobile** | Mobile‑size frames for each page |

This hierarchy mirrors the way developers think about responsive breakpoints, making handoff smoother later on.

### 2.5 Aligning and spacing frames automatically  

Even though we’ll dive deeper into grids later, you can already use **smart guides**:

- **Snap to pixel grid:** Toggle the **Snap to pixel grid** icon in the top toolbar.  
- **Distribute spacing:** Select multiple frames, then click the **Align and Distribute** icons that appear in the floating toolbar. Choose **Horizontal Distribute Center** to evenly space your frames across the canvas.

---

## 3. Layer Hierarchy Inside Frames  

### 3.1 Why a clean hierarchy matters  

Layers are the building blocks of any design. When they’re nested logically, you can:

- **Select** a whole section (e.g., navigation) with a single click.  
- **Hide** or **lock** groups while working on other parts.  
- **Export** assets without manually picking each element.

### 3.2 Basic hierarchy structure for a typical web page  

```
[Frame] Home – Desktop
 ├─ Header
 │   ├─ Logo
 │   ├─ Nav Menu
 │   └─ CTA Button
 ├─ Hero Section
 │   ├─ Background Image
 │   ├─ Heading
 │   └─ Subheading
 ├─ Content Grid
 │   ├─ Card 1
 │   ├─ Card 2
 │   └─ Card 3
 └─ Footer
     ├─ Links
     └─ Copyright
```

Each indented line represents a **layer** nested under its parent. You’ll build this hierarchy using **Groups** (shortcut **Ctrl/⌘ G**) and **Frames** when appropriate.

### 3.3 Creating groups and sub‑frames  

1. **Select multiple layers** you want to treat as a unit (e.g., all items in the navigation bar).  
2. Press **Ctrl/⌘ G** to group them. The group appears as a single layer in the **Layers** panel, with a folder icon.  
3. To further structure, you can **nest a frame inside a group** (or vice‑versa). For example, wrap the entire **Header** group inside its own **Header** frame. This gives you both the flexibility of a group (quick selection) and the properties of a frame (background color, constraints).

### 3.4 Naming conventions for layers  

Consistent naming speeds up searching and reduces miscommunication. A simple pattern:

```
[Section] – [Element] – [State]
```

Examples:  

- `Header – Logo – Default`  
- `Hero – Heading – Large`  
- `Card – Image – Hover`

When you type part of the name in the **search bar**, Figma instantly filters the layer list, letting you jump to the exact element you need.

### 3.5 Locking and hiding layers  

- **Lock:** Click the lock icon next to a layer to prevent accidental moves.  
- **Hide:** Click the eye icon to temporarily remove a layer from view.  

Use these tools while you’re focusing on a specific region of the page—e.g., lock the **Header** while you flesh out the **Content Grid**.

### 3.6 Using the **Move** tool for precise placement  

Even though you already know the **Move** tool, remember that it works on any selected layer or group. With a layer highlighted, you can:

- Nudge with arrow keys (hold **Shift** for 10‑pixel steps).  
- Drag while holding **Alt/Option** to duplicate the element instantly.  

These shortcuts become invaluable when you’re arranging repeated components like cards or list items inside a frame.

---

## 4. Practical Walk‑Through: From Blank File to Organized Prototype  

### 4.1 Scenario overview  

You’re designing a simple three‑page website for a boutique coffee shop. The client wants desktop, tablet, and mobile concepts for each page. Follow the steps below to set up a clean file structure before any visual design begins.

### 4.2 Step‑by‑step  

| Step | Action | Result |
|------|--------|--------|
| 1 | **Create a new file** from the **Dashboard**. | Blank canvas ready. |
| 2 | **Add three pages**: *Wireframes – Desktop*, *Wireframes – Tablet*, *Wireframes – Mobile*. Rename each accordingly. | Logical separation of device sizes. |
| 3 | On the *Desktop* page, **draw four frames** using the **Frame** tool with the **Desktop** preset: *Home*, *Menu*, *About*, *Contact*. | Four artboards ready for layout. |
| 4 | Switch to the *Tablet* page, repeat step 3 with the **Tablet** preset. | Consistent set of tablet frames. |
| 5 | Switch to the *Mobile* page, repeat step 3 with the **Mobile** preset. | Mobile frames complete. |
| 6 | Inside the *Home* desktop frame, **create a Header group**: add a **Logo** shape, a **Nav Menu** text layer, and a **CTA Button** shape. **Group** them and name the group `Header – Main`. | Header elements are bundled. |
| 7 | **Nest a Header frame** inside the group (optional) to give the header its own background color later. | Header now has its own frame properties. |
| 8 | **Repeat** for the Hero, Content Grid, and Footer sections, using the hierarchy shown in section 3.3. | Whole page is organized. |
| 9 | **Duplicate** the entire *Home* desktop frame (right‑click → Duplicate) and rename the copy *Home – Mobile*. Then **Resize** it to the mobile preset. | Mobile version of the home page ready for adaptation. |
|10 | **Lock** the Header group on all frames. | Prevents accidental shifts while you work on body content. |

By the end of this process you have a **file skeleton** that mirrors the client’s deliverables, with clear page separation, device‑specific frames, and a tidy layer hierarchy.

### 4.3 Quick sanity check  

- **Search test:** Type “Header” in the search bar. All header groups should appear, confirming consistent naming.  
- **Visibility test:** Hide the **Footer** layer on the desktop frame. The rest of the design should remain intact, showing that the hierarchy works as expected.  
- **Export test:** Select the **Header** frame, go to **Export** in the **Properties Panel**, and choose **PNG**. Figma should export only the header without the rest of the page, proving that your grouping is functional.

---

## 5. Tips for Scaling Your Project  

- **Template frames:** Once you’ve crafted a frame that matches your brand’s grid (later covered in Chapter 3), duplicate it for every new page. This guarantees uniform dimensions and saves time.  
- **Page color coding:** Right‑click a page and choose **Change color**. Assign a distinct hue to each design phase (e.g., light blue for Wireframes, teal for Mockups). The color appears as a subtle background strip, helping you spot the active page at a glance.  
- **Use comments wisely:** If you’re collaborating, drop a **Comment** on a specific frame to ask about a design decision. The comment will stay attached to that frame even if you later move it to another page.  
- **Version snapshots:** Before a major redesign, duplicate the current page (e.g., *Mockups – Desktop* → *Mockups – Desktop v2*). This creates a version history without needing external tools.

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why it happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **All frames on one page** | New users think pages are optional. | Create separate pages for each device or design phase early on. |
| **Unnamed layers** | Forgetting to rename after grouping. | Adopt the naming pattern from section 3.5 and rename immediately after creating a group. |
| **Over‑nesting frames** | Trying to mimic HTML hierarchy too literally. | Keep nesting to a maximum of 2‑3 levels; deeper structures become hard to navigate. |
| **Changing frame size after adding many layers** | Resizing a frame without adjusting inner elements leads to misalignment. | Use **Constraints** (covered later) or resize the frame first, then place content. |
| **Leaving duplicate pages unlocked** | Accidentally editing the wrong version. | Lock pages you’re not actively working on, or rename them with “(archived)”. |

---

## 7. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet  

- **Add page:** `Pages` panel → **+**  
- **Rename page:** Double‑click page name → type → **Enter**  
- **Duplicate page:** Right‑click → **Duplicate**  
- **Create device frame:** **F** → **Preset** dropdown → select size  
- **Custom frame size:** Draw → edit width/height in **Properties Panel**  
- **Group layers:** Select → **Ctrl/⌘ G**  
- **Rename layer:** Double‑click layer → type → **Enter**  
- **Lock layer:** Click lock icon in **Layers** panel  
- **Hide layer:** Click eye icon in **Layers** panel  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Pages** let you separate design phases and device versions; always name them with a clear convention.  
- **Frames** are your artboards; use preset device sizes or custom dimensions to match the target screens.  
- A **logical layer hierarchy**—sections → groups → elements—makes selection, editing, and exporting painless.  
- Build a **project skeleton** (pages → frames → organized layers) before adding visual detail; this foundation prevents clutter as the design grows.  
- Consistent naming, locking, and color‑coding are simple habits that dramatically improve workflow and collaboration.

modules.title: Layout Grids, Columns, and Guides
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Problem: The Header That Won’t Align  

You’ve just opened a fresh Figma file to design the homepage for a new tech startup. The brief says the header must contain a logo on the left, a navigation menu in the middle, and a call‑to‑action button on the right—*all* perfectly spaced, no matter whether the browser window is 1200 px wide or 320 px wide.  

Without a systematic way to divide the space, you’ll quickly find yourself guessing margins, moving objects back and forth, and wondering why the design looks “off” on different screen sizes. The answer lies in **layout grids**, **columns**, and **guides**—the invisible scaffolding that keeps web layouts consistent and adaptable.

Below we’ll walk through everything you need to set up a column grid, tweak its properties, and use rulers and guides for pixel‑perfect alignment. By the end, you’ll also understand the crucial distinction between **fixed** and **fluid** grids, so you can choose the right approach for any project.

---

## Understanding Layout Grids  

### What Is a Layout Grid?  
A **layout grid** is a set of invisible lines that you attach to a frame. These lines act as reference points for positioning objects, just like the ruled lines on a notebook page. Figma offers three grid types:

| Grid Type | Typical Use | Visual Shape |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|
| **Column** | Web pages, apps (horizontal division) | Vertical strips |
| **Row**    | Vertical rhythm, typographic baselines | Horizontal strips |
| **Grid**   | Complex layouts, print designs | Square cells |

For website prototyping we almost always start with a **column grid** because web designs are built from left to right.

### Fixed vs. Fluid Grids  

| Aspect | **Fixed Grid** | **Fluid (Stretch) Grid** |
|--------|----------------|--------------------------|
| **Definition** | Columns have a set pixel width; margins and gutters stay the same regardless of frame size. | Columns expand or shrink to fill the frame; margins stay constant while gutters stretch proportionally. |
| **When to Use** | When you need a precise, pixel‑perfect layout (e.g., a high‑fidelity mockup for a developer handoff). | When you want the design to respond to different screen widths without manually resizing every element. |
| **Behavior on Resize** | Columns may overflow or leave empty space if the frame becomes narrower or wider. | Columns always fill the available width, keeping the overall layout balanced. |

Think of a **fixed grid** like a set of rigid bookends—everything inside stays the same size. A **fluid grid** is more like a rubber band that stretches while keeping the outer edges anchored.

---

## Adding a Column Grid to a Frame  

You already know how to create a frame from the **Frames** tool (Chapter 2). Let’s turn that frame into a structured canvas.

1. **Select the frame** you want to work with (e.g., a desktop artboard 1440 × 1024 px).  
2. In the **Properties Panel** on the right, locate the **Layout grid** section under the **Design** tab.  
3. Click the **"+"** button. By default, Figma adds a **grid** (square cells).  
4. Click the grid icon that appears and switch the type to **Columns**.  

You’ll now see a series of vertical lines overlaying your frame. By default, Figma gives you a 12‑column grid with a 20 px gutter and 24 px margins, which matches many common web design systems.

### Adjusting Grid Properties  

Open the **Columns** settings by clicking the gear icon next to the grid name. You’ll see four main controls:

| Property | What It Does | Typical Values |
|----------|--------------|----------------|
| **Count** | Number of columns (e.g., 12) | 8 – 24 for most web layouts |
| **Gutter** | Space between columns | 16 px – 40 px (depends on design density) |
| **Margin** | Space between the outermost columns and the frame edge | 24 px – 120 px (often 1 × column width) |
| **Type** | **Fixed** or **Stretch** (fluid) | Choose based on the behavior you need |

#### Quick Example  

Suppose you’re designing a tablet layout (768 px wide) and want a 8‑column grid with a 24 px gutter and 32 px margins:

| Setting | Value |
|---------|-------|
| **Count** | 8 |
| **Gutter** | 24 px |
| **Margin** | 32 px |
| **Type** | **Stretch** (fluid) |

Enter these numbers, and Figma instantly recalculates the column widths to fill the frame while preserving the margins and gutter.

### Visual Confirmation  

- **Blue lines** = column edges.  
- **Dashed lines** = margins (if you enable “Show margins”).  

Toggle the visibility by clicking the eye icon next to the grid name. This helps you see whether objects are truly inside a column or spilling over a margin.

---

## Working with Rulers and Guides  

While grids give you a macro‑structure, **rulers** and **guides** help you nail down specific element positions—especially useful for aligning logos, icons, or custom spacing that doesn’t fit the column rhythm.

### Enabling Rulers  

1. From the top menu, choose **View → Show Rulers** (or press **Shift + R**).  
2. Rulers appear along the top and left edges of the canvas, displaying pixel measurements.

### Dragging Guides  

- **Vertical guide**: Click on the left ruler, drag rightward, and release where you want the guide.  
- **Horizontal guide**: Click on the top ruler, drag downward.

Guides snap to the nearest pixel by default. You can also **hold Shift** while dragging to lock the guide to **exact increments** (e.g., every 8 px) for consistent spacing.

### Aligning Objects to Guides  

When you move an object, Figma’s **smart guides** (the thin orange lines) appear automatically, indicating when the object’s edge or center aligns with a guide, another object, or a grid line.  

- **Snap to pixel**: Toggle this in **View → Snap to Pixel** for finer control.  
- **Lock a guide**: Right‑click a guide and choose **Lock Guide** to prevent accidental movement.

### Using Guides for Non‑Column Elements  

Imagine your logo needs a 48 px clearance from the top edge, regardless of the column structure. Drag a horizontal guide to **48 px** from the top ruler and snap the logo’s top edge to that guide. This technique ensures consistent spacing across different frames (desktop, tablet, mobile) without manually measuring each time.

---

## Practical Workflow: Building a Consistent Web Layout  

Let’s combine the tools we’ve just covered into a step‑by‑step workflow that mirrors a real design task.

### Scenario: Designing a Landing‑Page Header  

**Goal**: Create a header with three zones—logo, navigation, CTA button—aligned to a 12‑column grid on a desktop frame (1440 px wide).

#### Step 1 – Set Up the Frame  

- Create a new frame (desktop size) using the **Frame** tool.  
- Name it **“Header‑Desktop”** in the **Layers** panel for easy reference.

#### Step 2 – Apply a Column Grid  

- Select the frame, add a **Columns** layout grid.  
- Set **Count** = 12, **Gutter** = 24 px, **Margin** = 120 px, **Type** = **Fixed** (high‑fidelity mockup).  

You now have 12 equal columns, each 80 px wide (1440 – 2 × 120 – 11 × 24 ÷ 12 = 80 px).

#### Step 3 – Add Guides for Key Breakpoints  

- Turn on **Rulers**.  
- Drag a vertical guide to the edge of column 4 (columns 1‑4 = 4 × 80 + 3 × 24 = 332 px).  
- Drag another guide to the edge of column 9 (columns 1‑9 = 9 × 80 + 8 × 24 = 912 px).  

These guides mark the start of the navigation area (between columns 5‑8) and the start of the CTA button (column 9 onward).

#### Step 4 – Place the Logo  

- Use the **Shape** tool to draw a placeholder rectangle (or import the logo).  
- Snap its left edge to the **left margin** (120 px) and its top edge to a **horizontal guide** at **32 px** (common top padding).  

#### Step 5 – Build the Navigation Menu  

- Create a text layer for each menu item.  
- Select all menu items, then **Align Horizontal Center** to the vertical guide at column 6.5 (mid‑point between columns 5‑8).  
- Ensure the baseline of the text aligns with a **horizontal guide** at **48 px** from the top edge for consistent vertical rhythm.

#### Step 6 – Add the CTA Button  

- Draw a rectangle for the button.  
- Snap its left edge to the vertical guide at column 9 (912 px).  
- Align its vertical center with the navigation baseline.

#### Step 7 – Verify with Smart Guides  

- Move each element slightly; notice the orange smart guides appear when an edge aligns with a column line or guide.  
- If any element drifts, drag it back until the smart guide disappears—this indicates perfect alignment.

#### Step 8 – Test Responsiveness (Fluid Grid)  

- Duplicate the **Header‑Desktop** frame, rename it **“Header‑Tablet”** (768 × 1024 px).  
- In the duplicated frame, change the column grid **Type** to **Stretch** (fluid).  
- Observe how column widths automatically shrink while the margins (still 120 px) stay constant.  
- The logo, navigation, and button maintain their relative positions because they are anchored to columns and guides, not absolute pixel values.

### Why This Works  

- **Columns** give you a repeatable horizontal rhythm.  
- **Guides** let you fine‑tune spacing for elements that don’t fit the column width exactly (e.g., a logo that’s 48 px wide).  
- **Fixed vs. Fluid** grids let you switch between a pixel‑perfect desktop mockup and a responsive prototype without rebuilding the layout.

---

## Fixed vs. Fluid Grids in Prototyping  

### Visualizing the Difference  

1. **Fixed Grid**  
   - Columns stay at their defined pixel width.  
   - If you resize the frame to 1024 px, the outer margins stay at 120 px, but the columns may overflow the frame, causing horizontal scrollbars in a real browser.  

2. **Fluid Grid**  
   - Columns stretch to fill the new width while preserving the margin.  
   - The same 12‑column layout on a 1024 px frame will automatically recalculate column width to about 56 px, keeping the design balanced.

### When to Choose Which  

- **High‑Fidelity Designs for Development Handoff**  
  - Use **fixed** grids so developers see exact pixel dimensions for spacing, typography, and component sizes.  

- **Interactive Prototypes & Responsive Testing**  
  - Switch to **fluid** grids to see how the layout adapts. Combine this with **Constraints** (covered later) to define how objects should resize or stay anchored.

### Quick Experiment  

- Open any frame with a column grid.  
- In the **Layout grid** settings, toggle **Type** between **Fixed** and **Stretch**.  
- Drag the right edge of the frame inward.  
- Watch the column lines either stay the same width (fixed) or compress/expand (fluid).  

This live feedback is a powerful way to convince stakeholders that your design will behave well on various screen sizes.

---

## Tips & Common Pitfalls  

- **Don’t overload the grid**: 12 columns is a de‑facto standard for web; 16‑column grids are useful for dense data tables, but more columns increase visual noise.  
- **Lock guides after placement**: Right‑click a guide → **Lock Guide** to avoid accidental moves, especially when collaborating.  
- **Name your grids**: In the **Layout grid** panel, click the default “Grid 1” and rename it (e.g., “Desktop 12‑col”). This keeps the Layers panel tidy when you have multiple grids on one frame.  
- **Use the “Show margins” toggle**: It reveals the invisible margin area, helping you verify that no element bleeds outside the intended edge.  
- **Combine grids and constraints wisely**: A fluid grid alone won’t make objects resize; you still need to set constraints (covered later) for each element’s behavior.  
- **Check for accidental overflow**: After switching a grid to **Fixed**, zoom out and look for any elements that extend beyond the margin—they’ll cause scrollbars in the final product.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Layout grids** are the backbone of consistent web designs; a **column grid** divides the horizontal space into repeatable columns.  
- **Fixed grids** keep column widths constant, ideal for pixel‑perfect mockups; **fluid (stretch) grids** adapt column widths to the frame size, perfect for responsive prototypes.  
- Adding a column grid: select a frame → **Layout grid** → **+** → switch to **Columns** → adjust **Count, Gutter, Margin, Type**.  
- **Rulers** and **guides** provide precise, custom alignment beyond the column structure—great for logos, icons, and unique spacing.  
- Use **smart guides** and **snap to pixel** to ensure objects sit exactly on grid lines or guides.  
- A practical workflow: set up a frame, apply a 12‑column fixed grid for desktop, add guides for key breakpoints, place elements using both columns and guides, then duplicate and switch to a fluid grid to test responsiveness.  
- Remember to **lock guides**, **name your grids**, and **watch for overflow** when toggling between fixed and fluid modes.  

With these tools, you can craft clean, adaptable web layouts that look right on any screen—and you’ll have a solid foundation for the more advanced responsive techniques that come later in the book.

modules.title: Designing with Shapes, Text, and Styles
modules.content:
## A UI Element Comes to Life  

Imagine you’re designing the landing page for a new coffee‑shop app. The first thing users will see is a **hero banner**: a bold rectangle with a headline, a short paragraph, and a call‑to‑action button. With just a few clicks you can turn a blank canvas into that banner—no code required. In this chapter you’ll learn how to draw the rectangle, shape the text, and apply reusable color and effect styles so the hero looks polished and ready for the next step: turning it into a component.

---

## 1. Drawing the Building Blocks  

### 1.1 Selecting the Shape Tool  

1. Open the **Dashboard**, click **New File**, and you’ll be in the **Editor**.  
2. In the left‑hand toolbar locate the **Shape tools** (the icons for rectangle, line, and ellipse).  
3. Click the **Rectangle** icon or press **R** on your keyboard.  

> *Tip:* If you need a perfect square, hold **Shift** while you drag.

### 1.2 Creating a Rectangle  

1. Click anywhere on the canvas and drag to the desired size.  
2. Release the mouse button. A new **layer** appears in the **Layers** panel, automatically named “Rectangle 1”.  
3. With the rectangle still selected, look at the **Properties Panel** under the **Design** tab. Here you can edit dimensions directly (e.g., width = 1440 px, height = 400 px) or fine‑tune the X/Y position.

### 1.3 Editing Shape Properties  

- **Corner radius** – round the corners by entering a value (e.g., 8 px) or dragging the corner‑radius handle that appears on the shape.  
- **Stroke** – add an outline by toggling the **Stroke** switch. Choose a weight (e.g., 2 px) and a color from the swatch.  
- **Fill** – set the interior color. Click the fill swatch, then pick a hue from the color picker or type a hex code (e.g., `#F5E8D0`).  

All changes are instantly reflected on the canvas, and because the rectangle lives inside a **frame** (the page you created earlier), it will snap to any **layout grids** you’ve set up.

### 1.4 Drawing Circles and Lines  

- **Ellipse** (`O` shortcut): Click‑drag to draw a circle; hold **Shift** for a perfect circle.  
- **Line** (`L` shortcut): Click once to set the start point, move the cursor, then click again to set the end point.  

Both shapes appear as separate **layers** and can be edited with the same **Properties Panel** controls—stroke, fill, opacity, and effects.

### 1.5 Grouping Shapes  

If your hero banner needs a background rectangle plus a decorative circle, select both layers (hold **Shift** and click each), then press **Ctrl + G** (or **Cmd + G** on Mac) to **Group** them. The group behaves like a single object for moving, aligning, or applying a shared style later on.

---

## 2. Adding and Formatting Text  

### 2.1 Inserting a Text Layer  

1. With the **Text** tool selected (shortcut **T**), click inside the rectangle where you want the headline.  
2. Type your copy, e.g., “Wake Up to Fresh Brew”.  

A new **layer** called “Text 1” appears. Text layers are vector‑based, so they stay crisp at any size.

### 2.2 Basic Text Controls  

In the **Properties Panel** under the **Design** tab you’ll find:

| Control | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| **Font family** | Choose a typeface (e.g., *Inter*, *Roboto*, *Playfair Display*). |
| **Font style** | Toggle **Bold**, **Italic**, **Regular**, etc. |
| **Size** | Set the point size (e.g., 48 pt for a headline). |
| **Line height** | Controls vertical spacing between lines; set to **Auto** or a numeric value (e.g., 56 px). |
| **Letter spacing** | Adjusts horizontal space between characters (e.g., +2 px for a more open feel). |
| **Paragraph spacing** | Adds space after a paragraph, handy for separating headline from body copy. |

### 2.3 Aligning Text  

- **Horizontal alignment** (left, center, right) icons appear in the same panel.  
- Use the **Alignment** tools in the top toolbar (or press **Shift + A**) to align the text relative to its parent rectangle.  

### 2.4 Resizing and Auto‑Width  

When you type a long headline, Figma may wrap the text. To keep the text on a single line:

1. Select the text layer.  
2. In the **Properties Panel**, switch the **Resize** mode from **Auto Height** to **Auto Width**.  

Now the text box expands horizontally as you type, making it easier to control layout.

### 2.5 Working with Multiple Text Layers  

Add a subtitle and a button label by repeating the process. Name each layer descriptively (e.g., “Hero Headline”, “Hero Subtitle”, “CTA Label”)—clear naming helps later when you create **styles**.

---

## 3. Building a Color and Effect System  

### 3.1 Why Reusable Styles Matter  

Imagine you later decide to change the brand’s primary color from teal to orange. If you’ve applied that color manually to each rectangle, you’d have to edit every layer. **Styles** let you define a color once and reuse it across the file, so a single change propagates everywhere.

### 3.2 Creating Color Styles  

1. Select any object that already has the desired fill (e.g., the hero rectangle with `#F5E8D0`).  
2. In the **Properties Panel**, click the **four‑dot** icon next to the Fill swatch.  
3. Choose **Create style**.  
4. Give it a meaningful name, such as **Background / Light**.  

The new style appears in the **Assets** panel under **Color Styles**.  

#### Adding More Colors  

Repeat the steps for:

- **Primary / Brand** – e.g., `#D2691E` (coffee brown).  
- **Secondary / Accent** – e.g., `#FFC107` (amber).  
- **Text / Primary** – e.g., `#212121` (dark gray).  
- **Text / Secondary** – e.g., `#666666` (medium gray).  

### 3.3 Applying Color Styles  

Instead of selecting a raw hex value, click the **style** name from the dropdown. The fill updates instantly, and the layer now shows a small **style tag** indicating the applied color style.  

If you later edit the style (double‑click the style name in the **Assets** panel and change the color), every layer using that style updates automatically.

### 3.4 Creating Effect Styles  

Effects include **shadows**, **blurs**, and **layers**. For a subtle card‑like shadow:

1. Select the rectangle you want to give depth.  
2. In the **Properties Panel**, click **Effects** → **+** → **Drop shadow**.  
3. Set values (e.g., X = 0, Y = 4, Blur = 12, Opacity = 15%).  
4. Click the **four‑dot** icon next to the effect row and choose **Create style**.  
5. Name it **Shadow / Soft**.  

Now any element can adopt the same shadow by selecting the style from the **Effects** dropdown.

### 3.5 Organizing Styles  

- **Color Styles** and **Effect Styles** appear as separate sections in the **Assets** panel.  
- Drag styles to reorder them, or create folders (right‑click → **New folder**) to group related styles (e.g., *Brand Colors*, *Neutrals*).  

Consistent naming conventions (e.g., *Category / Variant*) make it easy to locate the right style later.

---

## 4. Putting It All Together – A Mini Hero Banner  

### 4.1 Assemble the Elements  

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Draw a **Rectangle** (1440 × 400 px) and apply the **Background / Light** color style. |
| 2 | Add a **Headline** text layer, set **Font family** to *Playfair Display*, **Size** = 48 pt, **Weight** = Bold, and apply **Text / Primary** color style. |
| 3 | Add a **Subtitle** text layer beneath the headline, use *Inter* at 18 pt, **Line height** = 28 px, and apply **Text / Secondary** style. |
| 4 | Create a **Button**: draw a small **Rectangle** (200 × 48 px), round the corners (radius = 8 px), fill with **Primary / Brand** color style, and add a **Label** text layer (“Order Now”) with **Text / Light** style. |
| 5 | Select the button rectangle and apply the **Shadow / Soft** effect style. |
| 6 | Group the button rectangle and its label (Ctrl + G). Position the group centrally under the subtitle. |

### 4.2 Quick Alignment Using Guides  

Because you already set up **layout grids** in Chapter 3, the hero rectangle snaps to the grid columns. Use **Zoom controls** (`Ctrl + ` or `Cmd + `) to fine‑tune placement, and the **Move** tool (shortcut **V**) to nudge objects by 1 px increments.

### 4.3 Testing Reusability  

Duplicate the entire hero (select the frame containing the rectangle, text, and button, then press **Alt + Drag**). The duplicate inherits all the same color and effect styles. Change the **Primary / Brand** color style from coffee brown to a teal (`#008080`). Instantly, both the original and duplicated hero buttons update, proving the power of reusable styles.

---

## 5. Best Practices for Beginners  

- **Name layers deliberately**: “Hero Background”, “Hero Headline”, “CTA Button”. Good names reduce friction when you later need to locate or edit a layer.  
- **Keep styles atomic**: One style per property (e.g., a “Primary / Brand” color style only controls fill, not stroke). This makes it easy to mix and match.  
- **Use the keyboard**: Shortcuts like **R**, **O**, **L**, **T**, **V**, **Ctrl + G**, **Alt + Drag** dramatically speed up workflow.  
- **Leverage Undo / Redo**: Don’t fear experimentation; Figma’s non‑linear history lets you revert any step.  
- **Stay organized**: Periodically clean the **Layers** panel—hide or delete unused shapes, rename ambiguous layers, and collapse groups you no longer need.

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why it Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Applying raw colors instead of styles** | It feels quicker to click a swatch. | Pause and check the **style** dropdown before applying a fill. |
| **Over‑nesting groups** | Grouping every tiny element creates a deep hierarchy that’s hard to navigate. | Group only when you need to move elements together; otherwise keep layers flat. |
| **Ignoring pixel‑perfect alignment** | Relying on visual judgment leads to off‑grid layouts. | Turn on **Snap to pixel grid** (found under **View** → **Snap to pixel grid**) and use the layout grid you set up earlier. |
| **Forgetting to name text layers** | “Text 1” gives no context when you revisit the file weeks later. | Rename immediately after creating a layer (double‑click the layer name). |
| **Using too many font variations** | Multiple fonts or weights increase visual noise. | Stick to a maximum of two typefaces per screen; use weight and size for hierarchy. |

---

## 7. Extending Your Skills  

Now that you can draw shapes, format text, and build a style system, the next logical step is to turn these elements into **components** (covered in Chapter 5). Components let you reuse the hero banner across multiple pages while maintaining a single source of truth for its design. When you’re ready, you’ll also explore how **constraints** keep your layout responsive.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Shapes are the canvas**: Use the Rectangle, Ellipse, and Line tools to create UI primitives; edit them via the **Properties Panel** (size, corner radius, stroke, fill).  
- **Text layers are vector**: Control typography with font family, size, line height, and letter spacing; align text using the same panel.  
- **Reusable styles save time**: Create **Color Styles** and **Effect Styles** (shadows, blurs) and apply them through the style dropdown; editing a style updates every instance instantly.  
- **Organize from the start**: Name layers descriptively, group only when needed, and keep your style library tidy with clear naming conventions.  
- **Practice the workflow**: Draw a rectangle, add headline and button text, apply color and effect styles, then duplicate to see the impact of a single style change.  

With these fundamentals, you now have the toolkit to craft polished UI elements that are both visually consistent and easy to maintain throughout your Figma projects.

modules.title: Building Components and Variants
modules.content:
## Turning a Button Into a Reusable Component  

Imagine you’re designing the homepage of a new SaaS product. The hero section needs a **Primary Call‑to‑Action** button that appears in three visual states: **Default**, **Hover**, and **Active**. Rather than copy‑pasting the same rectangle and text three times, you can capture the whole button as a single component and let Figma handle the state switches for you.  

### 1. Assemble the layers  

1. **Create the base shape** – Use the **Rectangle** tool to draw a 200 × 48 px button on the canvas.  
2. **Add the label** – With the **Text** tool, type “Get Started” and center it vertically and horizontally inside the rectangle.  
3. **Apply styles** – Choose the fill colour, stroke, corner radius, and text style you defined earlier (see *Designing with Shapes, Text, and Styles*).  

All three objects now sit together inside the same **frame** (the frame you created in the previous chapter). In the **Layers** panel you should see a hierarchy like:

```
Button / Primary
   ├─ Rectangle  (background)
   └─ Text       (label)
```

### 2. Convert the layers into a component  

1. **Select the frame** – Click the frame name “Button / Primary” in the Layers panel.  
2. **Create the component** – Press **⌘ + Alt + K** (Mac) or **Ctrl + Alt + K** (Windows).  
   - The frame border turns blue, indicating it is now a **Component**.  
   - In the **Assets** panel you’ll see a new entry with the same name.  

> **Tip:** Naming conventions matter. Rename the component to `Button/Primary` (use a slash to create a logical hierarchy) so it appears neatly in the library later.

### 3. Test the component instance  

Drag a copy of the component from the **Assets** panel onto the canvas. This copy is an **instance**—any change you make to the master component will automatically reflect here. Try editing the label text on the instance; you’ll see the master stays unchanged, proving the power of instances.

---

## Adding Variants for Interaction States  

A **variant** is a sibling component that shares the same underlying structure but differs in appearance or behaviour. Variants live inside a **variant set**, which Figma treats as a single component with configurable **properties** (e.g., `State = Default | Hover | Active`).  

### 1. Create the first variant (Default)  

Your newly‑made `Button/Primary` component already represents the **Default** state.  

1. With the component selected, click **+ Add variant** in the right‑hand **Properties** panel.  
2. Figma automatically creates a second component side‑by‑side and opens the **Properties** section.  

### 2. Define the property  

1. In the **Properties** panel, you’ll see a field labelled **Property 1**. Rename it to **State**.  
2. The first component shows `State = Default`.  
3. Click the second component and change its label to `State = Hover`.  

### 3. Style the Hover variant  

1. Select the Hover component.  
2. Change the rectangle’s fill colour (e.g., a slightly lighter shade).  
3. Optionally adjust the text colour or add a subtle drop‑shadow.  

### 4. Add the Active variant  

1. Click **+ Add variant** again.  
2. Rename the new component’s property value to `Active`.  
3. Style it (e.g., darker fill, pressed‑in effect).  

Now you have a three‑state variant set:

```
Button/Primary
   ├─ State = Default
   ├─ State = Hover
   └─ State = Active
```

### 5. Switching states in an instance  

1. Drag the `Button/Primary` component onto a new frame.  
2. In the **Properties** panel for that instance, you’ll see a dropdown for **State**.  
3. Choose **Hover** – the instance instantly updates to the Hover styling.  

> **Why it matters:** When you later add interaction prototypes, you’ll simply toggle the `State` property instead of creating separate layers for each visual change.

---

## Organizing Components in a Shared Library  

When a team works on multiple pages or files, you don’t want each designer to rebuild the same button over and over. Figma lets you publish a **team library** that any file in the same project can consume.  

### 1. Set up a dedicated “Design System” file  

1. From the **Dashboard**, click **New File** and name it **Design System**.  
2. Inside this file, create a **Page** called **Components** (use the **Pages** panel).  
3. Paste your `Button/Primary` component (and any other UI pieces) onto this page.  

### 2. Publish the library  

1. Open the **Assets** panel → click the **Library** icon (bookshelf).  
2. At the bottom, select **Publish**.  
3. Review the list of components; you’ll see `Button/Primary` listed.  
4. Click **Publish** to make the library available to everyone in the team.  

> **Note:** Publishing does not lock the components. Designers can still create local overrides; the master component remains the single source of truth.

### 3. Enable the library in other files  

1. Open any design file (e.g., the homepage mock‑up).  
2. In the **Assets** panel, click the **Library** icon.  
3. Toggle the switch next to **Design System** to **On**.  
4. The `Button/Primary` component now appears under **Team Library** in the Assets panel.  

### 4. Best practices for library hygiene  

- **Group by category** – Use slashes in component names (`Button/Primary`, `Button/Secondary`, `Form/Input`) so the Assets panel automatically nests them.  
- **Version control** – When you change a component (e.g., update the colour palette), publish a new version. Team members will see a **Update library** prompt, ensuring everyone works with the latest design language.  
- **Document usage** – Add a simple **Description** field in the component’s **Properties** panel (e.g., “Primary CTA, used for main actions”). This shows up in the library panel and helps newcomers pick the right component.  

---

## Quick Workflow: From Sketch to Production‑Ready Component  

1. **Sketch** – Roughly draw the UI element on a **Frame** using shape and text tools.  
2. **Style** – Apply colours, typography, and effects.  
3. **Componentize** – Select the frame and hit **⌘ + Alt + K**.  
4. **Variantize** – Add as many variants as needed (Default, Hover, Active, Disabled, etc.).  
5. **Publish** – Store the component in a shared library.  
6. **Consume** – Drag instances from the library into any design file, toggle properties to match the required state.  

This loop keeps the design system lean, reduces duplication, and speeds up handoff to developers (who can reference the same component names when coding).

---

## Managing Component Variants at Scale  

When a product grows, the number of variants can explode (e.g., a button may have size variants: Small, Medium, Large). Figma lets you combine multiple properties in a single variant set.  

### Example: Adding a **Size** property  

1. Select the `Button/Primary` variant set.  
2. Click **+ Add property** → name it **Size**.  
3. For each existing state (Default, Hover, Active), duplicate the row and set **Size = Small**, **Size = Medium**, **Size = Large**.  
4. Adjust the rectangle dimensions and text size accordingly.  

Now an instance shows two dropdowns: **State** and **Size**, letting designers mix‑and‑match any combination without creating separate components for each permutation.  

> **Performance tip:** Keep the total number of variants under 30‑40. If you need more, consider breaking the component into smaller parts (e.g., a separate “Icon Button” component) and combine them with **Auto Layout** later (covered in a future chapter).

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why it Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Over‑naming components** – using long, descriptive names for each variant | Makes the Assets panel cluttered and hard to search | Use concise property values (`State=Hover`) and rely on the **Properties** panel to convey meaning |
| **Editing an instance instead of the master** | Mistakenly thinks changes are global | Double‑click the component name in the Layers panel or use **Shift + ⌘ + K** to “Detach instance” only when you truly need a one‑off variation |
| **Publishing incomplete components** | Team members receive half‑finished UI pieces | Run a quick checklist before publishing: naming, states, documentation, and visual consistency |
| **Missing property values** – forgetting to set a default for a new property | Instances default to an empty state, causing unexpected appearance | After adding a new property, always set one of the variants as the **Default** (the one with the check‑mark in the Properties panel) |

---

## Bringing It All Together: A Mini‑Project  

> **Scenario:** You’re tasked with designing a sign‑up form that includes a **Submit** button, a **Cancel** button, and a **Password visibility toggle**.  

1. **Create three base components** – `Button/Primary`, `Button/Secondary`, `Icon/Visibility`.  
2. **Add state variants** – For each button, add **Default**, **Hover**, **Active**; for the visibility icon, add **Shown** and **Hidden**.  
3. **Publish** the components to the **Design System** library.  
4. **Assemble the form** – Drag the components onto a new frame, set the appropriate state properties, and you have a fully interactive mock‑up ready for prototyping (next chapter).  

By the end of this exercise you will have a small, reusable UI kit that can be expanded as the product evolves.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- Converting a group of layers into a **Component** creates a single source of truth that can be reused across files.  
- **Variants** let you capture multiple visual states (e.g., Default, Hover, Active) within one component, controlled through **properties** like `State`.  
- Publishing components to a **team library** makes them accessible to every designer, fostering consistency and reducing duplicated effort.  
- Organize component names with slashes (`Button/Primary`) to keep the Assets panel tidy and to enable logical categorization.  
- Combine multiple properties (e.g., `State` and `Size`) to manage complex UI elements without exploding the number of separate components.  
- Follow naming conventions, set defaults, and document each component to maintain a healthy design system as the project scales.

modules.title: Linking Screens and Creating Basic Prototypes
modules.content:
## From Static Mock‑up to Clickable Flow  

Imagine you’ve just finished a clean homepage design for a boutique coffee shop. The layout looks great, the typography is spot‑on, and the brand colors are consistent across the **frames** you created in the **Editor**. But a client asks, “Can I see how the site will feel when a user clicks ‘Menu’ or ‘Contact’?” That’s where prototyping steps in. By linking your frames with simple click interactions, you turn a collection of static screens into a navigable mock‑up that can be presented, tested, and iterated on—without writing a single line of code.

In this chapter you’ll learn how to:

* Connect frames with click interactions to simulate navigation.
* Choose from the core transition types—**Dissolve**, **Slide**, and **Instant**—and understand when each feels natural.
* Preview your prototype in **Presentation mode** so you can walk through the flow just as a real user would.

All of this builds directly on the frames, layers, and components you assembled in earlier chapters, so you’ll see how the pieces fit together.

---

## 1. Setting the Stage: Organize Your Screens  

Before you start linking, make sure your design files are ready for prototyping.

### 1.1. Name Your Frames Clearly  

A tidy naming convention helps you locate the right destination when you create a link.

* **Home** – the landing page.
* **Menu** – the coffee menu screen.
* **Contact** – the contact form.

You can rename a frame by selecting it in the **Layers** panel and typing a new name. Consistent names also appear in the prototyping panel, reducing the chance of linking to the wrong screen.

### 1.2. Group Related Screens on a Single Page  

If you’re working on a multi‑page website, keep all related screens on one **Page** (e.g., “Coffee Shop Site”). This keeps the **Dashboard** tidy and makes it easier to toggle between design and prototype views.

### 1.3. Verify Component States  

If you built a navigation bar as a **Component** with variants for “default” and “hover,” ensure each variant is placed on the appropriate frame. The prototype will respect the visual state you see in the design view.

---

## 2. Adding Interaction Triggers  

Figma’s prototyping workflow revolves around **interaction triggers**—the events that start a transition. The most common trigger for website navigation is **On Click**.

### 2.1. Open the Prototype Tab  

Select any layer (e.g., a button or a navigation link) and switch from the **Design** tab to the **Prototype** tab in the right‑hand sidebar. If you don’t see the tab, make sure you’re not in the **Comment** mode.

### 2.2. Create a Connection  

1. **Select the source element** (e.g., the “Menu” text link).  
2. **Drag the blue node** (a small circular handle) that appears on the right side of the element onto the destination frame (e.g., the **Menu** screen).  
3. A gray line will appear, indicating a connection.

### 2.3. Define the Interaction  

When the node is connected, a small **Interaction Details** panel pops up. Fill in the fields:

| Field | Typical Value for Navigation |
|-------|------------------------------|
| **Trigger** | **On Click** (default) |
| **Action** | **Navigate To** |
| **Destination** | Choose the target frame (e.g., *Menu*) |
| **Animation** | Pick a transition type (see next section) |
| **Preserve Scroll Position** | *Off* for most page‑to‑page flows |

If you need a different trigger—like **While Hovering** for a tooltip—select it from the dropdown. For now, stick with **On Click** to keep the flow straightforward.

### 2.4. Linking Multiple Elements  

Repeat the steps for each navigation element:

| Source | Destination |
|--------|-------------|
| Home → Menu | Menu |
| Home → Contact | Contact |
| Menu → Home | Home |
| Contact → Home | Home |

A quick tip: after you create one link, you can **duplicate** it by holding **Alt** (Windows) or **Option** (macOS) while dragging the blue node to a new destination. This speeds up repetitive linking.

---

## 3. Choosing Transition Types  

When a user clicks a link, the screen change can happen in several ways. Figma offers three core transition styles that work well for most website prototypes.

### 3.1. Instant  

*What it does:* The new frame appears immediately, with no animation.  

*When to use it:*  
- For simple, static pages where the change feels like a traditional page load.  
- When you want to emphasize speed or when the design already contains its own motion (e.g., a loading spinner).  

*How to set it:* In the **Animation** dropdown, select **Instant**. No additional settings are needed.

### 3.2. Dissolve  

*What it does:* The current frame fades out while the next frame fades in, creating a smooth cross‑fade.  

*When to use it:*  
- When moving between pages that share a similar visual hierarchy, such as “Home → About.”  
- To give a subtle cue that the user is still within the same site context.  

*How to set it:*  
1. Choose **Dissolve** from the **Animation** dropdown.  
2. Adjust the **Duration** (default 300 ms). A shorter duration feels snappier; a longer one feels more cinematic.

### 3.3. Slide  

*What it does:* The new frame slides in from a direction (left, right, up, or down) while the current frame slides out.  

*When to use it:*  
- For mobile‑first designs where a horizontal swipe feels natural.  
- To simulate a carousel or a wizard‑style flow (e.g., “Step 1 → Step 2”).  

*How to set it:*  
1. Pick **Slide In** from the **Animation** dropdown.  
2. Choose a **Direction** (Left, Right, Up, Down).  
3. Set the **Easing** (e.g., **Ease Out**) to control the acceleration curve.  
4. Tweak the **Duration** to match the desired speed.

### 3.4. Quick Decision Checklist  

| Situation | Recommended Transition |
|-----------|------------------------|
| Simple page navigation (desktop) | **Dissolve** |
| Mobile swipe or wizard steps | **Slide** |
| Immediate jump (e.g., login redirect) | **Instant** |

Keeping this checklist handy helps you choose the right feel without over‑thinking each link.

---

## 4. Previewing the Prototype  

Now that your frames are linked and transitions set, it’s time to test the flow.

### 4.1. Enter Presentation Mode  

1. Click the **Present** button (a play‑icon) located at the top‑right of the **Editor** window.  
2. A new browser‑like window opens, starting from the first frame on the current page.  

If you need to start from a different screen, simply select that frame before hitting **Present**, or use the **Prototype Settings** panel (gear icon) to set a custom starting point.

### 4.2. Interact Like a User  

Navigate through the prototype by clicking the links you created. Pay attention to:

* **Transition smoothness** – does the animation feel natural?  
* **Clickable areas** – are the hit zones (the invisible clickable region) correctly sized?  
* **State changes** – if you built hover or active variants, do they appear when expected?

### 4.3. Use the Device Preview  

Figma lets you simulate different device frames (e.g., iPhone, desktop monitor). Click the **Device** dropdown in the Presentation toolbar and choose a preset. This is especially useful when you later explore responsive design, but even now it helps you see how the prototype looks on a real‑world screen size.

### 4.4. Sharing the Prototype  

When you’re satisfied, click **Share Prototype** (the chain‑link icon) to generate a shareable link. You can set permissions to **Anyone with the link** or restrict it to specific collaborators. This link can be sent to stakeholders, who can view the flow in a web browser without needing a Figma account.

---

## 5. Fine‑Tuning Interactions  

Even a simple prototype can benefit from a few polish steps.

### 5.1. Adjust Hit Areas  

If a button feels hard to click, enlarge its hit area:

1. Select the button layer.  
2. In the **Prototype** tab, click **+** under **Interaction** to add a **Hotspot**.  
3. Drag the hotspot’s edges to cover a larger invisible rectangle.  

The visual appearance of the button remains unchanged, but the clickable region expands.

### 5.2. Preserve Scroll Position  

When linking between long pages (e.g., a scrolling “About” page), you might want the scroll position to stay where the user left off. In the **Interaction Details**, toggle **Preserve Scroll Position** *On*. This prevents the destination frame from snapping back to the top on each navigation.

### 5.3. Add a Back Button  

A common navigation pattern is a **Back** arrow that returns the user to the previous screen. Create a simple left‑arrow shape, turn it into a component (if you haven’t already), and link it to the appropriate previous frame using the same **On Click → Navigate To** workflow.

### 5.4. Test on Multiple Devices  

Even though this chapter doesn’t cover constraints or auto‑layout, you can still preview how the prototype behaves on different screen sizes. Use the **Zoom** controls in Presentation mode to shrink or enlarge the view, and verify that elements don’t disappear or overlap unexpectedly.

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Symptom | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| **Forgot to set the trigger** | Clicking does nothing. | Ensure the **Trigger** is set to **On Click** (or another appropriate event). |
| **Link points to the wrong frame** | Navigation goes to an unexpected screen. | Double‑check the **Destination** in the Interaction Details. Rename frames clearly to avoid confusion. |
| **Transition feels too slow** | Users wait too long for the next screen. | Reduce the **Duration** (e.g., from 300 ms to 150 ms). |
| **Hotspot is too small** | Clicks miss the intended target. | Expand the hotspot or use the **Auto Layout** (covered later) to ensure the button’s bounding box matches its visual size. |
| **Prototype starts on the wrong screen** | Presentation opens on a middle screen instead of Home. | Select the desired start frame before clicking **Present**, or set it explicitly in the **Prototype Settings** panel. |

By catching these issues early, you keep the prototype smooth and professional.

---

## 7. Quick Recap of the Workflow  

1. **Prepare frames** – name them and keep related screens on the same page.  
2. **Select a source element** and drag its blue node to the destination frame.  
3. **Set the interaction** to **On Click → Navigate To**, choose a transition (Dissolve, Slide, Instant), and adjust duration/easing as needed.  
4. **Preview** in Presentation mode, test all links, and tweak hit areas or scroll behavior.  
5. **Share** the prototype link with stakeholders for feedback.

Following this loop lets you transform static mock‑ups into an interactive experience that can be reviewed, tested, and iterated upon—all within the same Figma file.

---

## Key Takeaways  

* **Linking frames** with the blue node creates navigation paths; the default trigger is **On Click**.  
* **Transition types**—Instant, Dissolve, and Slide—provide three distinct motion cues; choose based on context (speed, device, flow).  
* **Presentation mode** lets you experience the prototype as a real user, test interactions, and share a live link for stakeholder review.  
* Small adjustments—hit‑area hotspots, scroll preservation, and proper naming—prevent common usability hiccups.  

With these tools you can now produce clickable, high‑fidelity prototypes that communicate your design intent far more effectively than static screenshots alone. The next chapter will show you how to make those prototypes responsive using constraints and Auto Layout. Happy prototyping!

modules.title: Responsive Design with Constraints and Auto Layout
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Challenge: Making a Navigation Bar Work on Any Screen  

Imagine you’ve just finished designing a sleek homepage for a new startup. The hero section looks perfect on a desktop monitor, but when you shrink the browser window to a tablet width, the navigation links spill out of the frame, and the logo gets cut off. A client asks, “Can we see how this will look on a phone?”  

The answer lies in two powerful Figma features you’ve already glimpsed: **constraints** and **auto layout**. By teaching the elements in your design how they should behave when their container changes size, you can prototype a single layout that adapts gracefully from large screens to tiny ones. The following sections walk you through applying constraints, building auto‑layout stacks, and testing responsiveness—step by step, with no prior knowledge assumed.

---

## 1. Why Constraints Matter  

When you created frames in **Chapter 2**, you gave each screen a fixed size (e.g., 1440 × 1024 px). Inside those frames, objects such as a logo, navigation links, and a search icon sit at specific coordinates. If the frame’s dimensions change, those objects stay where they were, which often leads to overlapping or disappearing elements.

**Constraints** tell Figma how an object should stay positioned relative to its **parent frame** (or to the nearest auto‑layout group). Think of them as invisible “rules” that say:

* “Keep this element **centered** horizontally.”
* “Maintain a **fixed distance** from the **right** edge.”
* “Stretch to fill the available **width** while keeping a constant **height**.”

When you resize the parent, Figma automatically recalculates the child’s position based on those rules. This is the first line of defense for responsive design.

### 1.1 Core Constraint Options  

| Option | What It Does | Typical Use Cases |
|--------|--------------|-------------------|
| **Left / Right / Top / Bottom** | Keeps a fixed distance from the chosen edge(s). | Buttons anchored to a corner, footer bars. |
| **Center** (horizontal or vertical) | Keeps the element centered along the chosen axis. | Logos, central headings. |
| **Scale** | Proportionally resizes the element as the parent grows or shrinks. | Decorative shapes that should maintain aspect ratio. |
| **Left & Right (or Top & Bottom)** | Stretches the element to fill the space between two edges. | Input fields, background rectangles. |

When you first encounter a constraint, the term **parent** refers to the immediate frame or group that contains the object. If the object lives inside an auto‑layout group, the group itself becomes the parent.

---

## 2. Applying Constraints Step‑by‑Step  

Below is a practical walk‑through using the navigation bar from our opening scenario. Follow each step in the **Editor**—the same workspace you used for creating shapes and text in earlier chapters.

### 2.1 Set Up the Frame  

1. **Create a new frame** (press **F**) and name it `NavBar – Desktop`.  
2. Size it to **1440 × 80 px** (standard desktop header height).  
3. Turn on a **layout grid** (Column count: 12, Gutter: 20 px, Margin: 40 px) to give yourself visual alignment guides. This mirrors the grid you learned in Chapter 3.

### 2.2 Add the Elements  

1. **Logo** – Use the **Text** tool to type the brand name, then style it with the font and color you defined in Chapter 4.  
2. **Nav Links** – Create a horizontal list of text layers (`Home`, `Features`, `Pricing`, `Contact`).  
3. **Search Icon** – Insert a simple vector shape (e.g., a magnifying glass) using the **Pen** tool.  

Group the three logical sections:

* `Logo` → **Group** (Ctrl/Cmd + G)  
* `Nav Links` → **Group** (this will later become an auto‑layout group)  
* `Search Icon` → **Group**  

Now you have three top‑level layers inside the `NavBar – Desktop` frame.

### 2.3 Assign Constraints  

Select each top‑level group and look at the **Constraints** panel in the right sidebar.

| Element | Constraint Settings | Reason |
|---------|---------------------|--------|
| **Logo** | **Left** & **Center‑Vertical** | Keeps the logo flush with the left margin while staying vertically centered. |
| **Nav Links** | **Center‑Horizontal** & **Center‑Vertical** | Centers the navigation horizontally, regardless of screen width. |
| **Search Icon** | **Right** & **Center‑Vertical** | Pins the icon to the right edge, staying centered vertically. |

> **Tip:** If you don’t see the Constraints panel, click the **“>”** icon next to the **Design** tab.  

Now, test the behavior:

1. Select the `NavBar – Desktop` frame.  
2. Drag its right edge leftward to simulate a tablet width (≈ 768 px).  
3. Observe: the logo stays glued to the left, the search icon hugs the right, and the nav links remain centered—no overlap occurs.

### 2.4 Stretching Elements with “Left & Right”
